  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yutong Xin
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models have achieved striking results in interactive theorem proving, particularly in Lean. However, most benchmarks for LLM-based proof automation are drawn from mathematics in the Mathlib ecosystem, whereas proofs in software verification are developed inside definition-rich codebases with substantial project-specific libraries. We introduce VeriSoftBench, a benchmark of 500 Lean 4 proof obligations drawn from open-source formal-methods developments and packaged to preserve realistic repository context and cross-file dependencies. Our evaluation of frontier LLMs and specialized provers yields three observations. First, provers tuned for Mathlib-style mathematics transfer poorly to this repository-centric setting. Second, success is strongly correlated with transitive repository dependence: tasks whose proofs draw on large, multi-hop dependency closures are less likely to be solved. Third, providing curated context restricted to a proof’s dependency closure improves performance relative to exposing the full repository, but nevertheless leaves substantial room for improvement. Our benchmark and evaluation suite are released at <a href="https://github.com/utopia-group/VeriSoftBench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">https://github.com/utopia-group/VeriSoftBench</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Large Language Models, ICML
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>Equal contribution</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Interactive theorem provers (ITPs) such as Lean <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moura and Ullrich, 2021</a>)</cite>, Rocq/Coq <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">The Coq Development Team, 2008</a>)</cite>, and Isabelle <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wenzel et al., 2008</a>)</cite> provide machine-checked guarantees, but this rigor comes with a well-known cost: even routine mathematical arguments require low-level, often tedious formalization, making mechanized proof development extremely labor-intensive. To reduce this burden, decades of work have pursued automation within ITP workflows, for example, using domain-specific tactic libraries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gladshtein et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rossel, 2024</a>)</cite> or integration with external solvers (e.g., SMT/ATP backends) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mohamed et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paulson and Blanchette, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. More recently, large language models (LLMs) have enabled a new class of <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">neural</em> proof automation methods, including systems specialized for Lean proof generation and repair <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Varambally et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These advances have made high-quality benchmark datasets crucial for further progress, as improvement depends not only on model quality, but also on benchmarks that reflect the proof settings where automation is ultimately needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Most widely used Lean benchmarks for LLM-based proof automation are drawn largely from <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">mathematics</em> and operate in a shared ecosystem centered around Mathlib. For example, suites such as MiniF2F <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, ProofNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azerbayev et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, LeanDojo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and PutnamBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tsoukalas et al., 2024</a>)</cite> have been instrumental in measuring progress and driving rapid improvements in proof automation for mathematics. However, in contrast to these benchmarks, proofs in software verification and programming-language meta-theory are typically developed inside large repositories that introduce their own core abstractions, definitions, and libraries. Proof obligations in this setting often hinge on nontrivial cross-file structure and on project-specific concepts. This raises a key question: <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">How well do current provers generalize when proofs are grounded in large, project-specific libraries rather than a shared ecosystem?</em></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18307v1/mot.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/206;" width="476" height="206" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Contextual dependencies comparison between (a) mathematical benchmark proofs, (b) lightweight verification tasks, and (c) repository-scale verification. PutnamBench proofs rely almost entirely on library (Mathlib) dependencies (purple). Verina introduces a small number of project-specific definitions (yellow) but remains largely library-driven. In contrast, proofs from a real-world ZK circuit DSL repository <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Verified-zkEVM, 2025</a>)</cite> depend heavily on interconnected local abstractions, forming a dense repository-level dependency graph. Purple denotes library dependencies; yellow denotes local/repository dependencies.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address this gap, this paper introduces VeriSoftBench, a benchmark of 500 Lean 4 proof obligations drawn from open-source formal-methods developments and packaged to preserve local context and multi-module structure, including cross-file dependencies. The benchmark is designed to evaluate provers in the regime that is common in verification and PL meta-theory, where proofs are often stated in terms of project-defined abstractions and typically require navigating internal libraries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A central goal of VeriSoftBench is to make the role of repository context explicit and measurable. We therefore evaluate provers under two context regimes. In the <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">curated</em> regime, the prover is provided with a focused set of repository dependencies associated with the ground-truth proof. In the <em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full-repository</em> regime, the prover is exposed to the entire local repository context. These two regimes allow us to separate challenges that arise from operating over large repositories from those that persist even when the relevant dependencies are provided.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments yield three main findings. First, provers that perform well on Mathlib-centric mathematics tasks transfer poorly to this repository-grounded setting. Second, performance degrades as <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">transitive</em> dependency structure increases, such as when discharging a goal requires reasoning over a large, multi-hop closure of project-local definitions and lemmas. Third, curated context improves over full-repository context, but there is substantial room for improvement even when the minimal relevant context is provided to the prover. This highlights that relevant context retrieval is necessary but not sufficient for successful proof automation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce VeriSoftBench, a benchmark of 500 Lean 4 proof obligations drawn from open-source formal-methods repositories, packaged to preserve repository context and cross-file dependencies.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide an evaluation of frontier LLMs and specialized provers under curated and full-repository context regimes, analyzing the relationship between prover success and structural properties of repository dependence.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Motivation</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ITPs such as Lean support <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">tactic-based</em> proof development: the user (or an automated prover) constructs a proof by applying a sequence of tactics that transform a proof state into simpler subgoals until all goals are discharged.
For LLM-based provers, the core task is therefore to generate a tactic script that discharges the goal and is accepted by Lean under the given local context and imports.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Much of the recent progress in Lean proof automation has been evaluated on mathematics-oriented benchmarks.
Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a) illustrates this regime using a PutnamBench task and a proof generated by SeedProver. While the proof is lengthy, its key references are primarily to Mathlib definitions and lemmas, reflecting a setting where the prover can rely on a stable, widely shared collection of abstractions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Proofs arising in software verification and programming-languages semantics often have a very different character. Rather than involving a fixed set of standard abstractions (as in Mathlib), these projects introduce custom datatypes, operations, and invariants that formalize the semantics or correctness criteria of the artifact being verified (e.g., a compiler pass, a program logic, or a domain-specific language).
For instance, Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(c) shows a representative example from a real Lean formal-methods repository: both the statement and the proof are densely populated with project-defined notions, and the supporting facts needed to complete the proof are distributed across the surrounding codebase. Existing verification-oriented benchmarks move in this direction but often at more modest scale: Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b) shows an example from a previous dataset called Verina <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>)</cite> that involves limited introduction of project-specific context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This shift from mathematical proofs to software verification tasks has two practical consequences that make proof automation more challenging in some respects. First, the prover must adapt to a <em id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">local logical environment</em>: many of the required definitions and lemmas are not part of Mathlib and are specific to the project, so success depends on correctly interpreting and using in-repository abstractions. Second, the available context is typically large and multi-module, yet only a small fraction is relevant to the goal. As such, effective proof search hinges on identifying the right local facts and using them inside the target proof script.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2 Background and Motivation ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> gives an overview of existing datasets in light of this discussion. Existing benchmark suites fall short in at least one respect, such as lacking project-specific definitions, multi-module context, or ground-truth proofs for systematic evaluation. Mathematics benchmarks such as MiniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench largely operate within a shared Mathlib ecosystem and do not stress project-local abstractions. LeanDojo draws from a large formal development and provides proofs, but its “project” is Mathlib itself rather than a collection of independent verification codebases with bespoke APIs. On the verification side, FVAPPS and CLEVER focus on verified code generation but are not designed around project-specific libraries, while Verina and MiniCodeProps introduce some local context but do not model the multi-module, codebase-level dependency structure illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(c). These gaps motivate VeriSoftBench, which is constructed to preserve project-specific definitions and cross-file dependencies and to support evaluation in a setting where codebase-local context is crucial for the proof task.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S2.T1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S2.T1.3.1" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#ECECEC;">

<td id="S2.T1.3.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;"><span id="S2.T1.3.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#AD0303;">✗</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;"><span id="S2.T1.3.3.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#AD0303;">✗</span></td>
<td id="S2.T1.3.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;"><span id="S2.T1.3.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#AD0303;">✗</span></td></tr>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Comparison of theorem proving benchmarks across domains and contextual requirements. Note that while LeanDojo satisfies the listed criteria, its scope is confined to the singular environment of Mathlib; on the other hand, VeriSoftBench features 23 diverse repositories with bespoke contexts.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>VeriSoftBench</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">VeriSoftBench is a benchmark of 500 Lean 4 proof obligations drawn from real, open-source formal-methods developments. Each task is extracted from a fixed Git commit and packaged to preserve the original proof environment, including project-specific abstractions and cross-file dependencies.
Unlike prior benchmarks that normalize tasks into a shared library setting, VeriSoftBench evaluates provers on theorems as they appear in the wild. That is, theorems are phrased in terms of project-defined datatypes and invariants, and completing the proof requires reasoning within the surrounding codebase.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Dataset Construction</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Benchmark Collection.</em> The benchmark is drawn from a diverse set of 23 Lean repositories, covering compiler correctness, programming language semantics and type systems, verification frameworks, and applied verification projects (e.g., zero-knowledge circuits, protocols, and optimization problems). Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Dataset Construction ‣ 3 VeriSoftBench ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the distribution of these repositories across topics.</p>
</div>

style="--ltx-fo-width:5.98em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="82.68"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.F2.pic1.7" class="ltx_text">Applied verif.</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#7FBF9B;" fill="#7FBF9B" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-width="0.8pt"><path d="M 89.9 2.1 h 9.22 v 9.22 h -9.22 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 104.56 1.91)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:4.96em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="68.69"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.F2.pic1.8" class="ltx_text">Framework</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#E6C46A;" fill="#E6C46A" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-width="0.8pt"><path d="M 89.9 -17.58 h 9.22 v 9.22 h -9.22 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 104.56 -17.7)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:4.39em;--ltx-fo-height:0.68em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="9.46" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.46)" width="60.81"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.F2.pic1.9" class="ltx_text">Semantics</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#FFFFFF;--ltx-fill-color:#C9A07A;" fill="#C9A07A" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-width="0.8pt"><path d="M 89.9 -37.27 h 9.22 v 9.22 h -9.22 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 104.56 -36.04)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:6.29em;--ltx-fo-height:0.68em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.15" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.46)" width="87.1"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.F2.pic1.10" class="ltx_text">Type systems
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g></svg></span>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Lean repository distribution across topics</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Benchmark Selection.</em>
When selecting benchmarks, we require each task to have a <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">valid</em> proof. This means that the ground-truth proof script should contain no proof holes (e.g., <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">sorry</span> or <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">admit</span>), and any lemmas or theorems it invokes are themselves recursively proven by hole-free scripts. In addition, the Lean file containing the target theorem must compile after replacing the ground-truth proof with <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">by sorry</span>, ensuring that the statement, imports, and required definitions are well-formed independently of the original proof term. Finally, we exclude trivial goals by requiring that the theorem is not discharged solely by standard automation (e.g., <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">simp</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">omega</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">grind</span>) and that it references at least one repository-local definition.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond enforcing validity, we select tasks that span a range of difficulty metrics. To this end, we score each benchmark along two axes: <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">proof complexity</em>, approximated by the length of the repository’s ground-truth tactic script, and <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">contextual dependency</em>, measured by how many distinct definitions and lemma statements the proof draws from repository-local files.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, VeriSoftBench is constructed by first filtering candidate theorems for validity and non-triviality, and then sampling 500 tasks from the remaining pool to balance repository category and the two difficulty axes described above.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18307v1/task.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:634/192;" width="634" height="192"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An example task instance from our benchmark. The goal is to synthesize a proof for the target theorem <span id="S3.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cexec_to_reds</span>, which relates two definitions of program execution in a formalized programming language. The figure illustrates the context that must be provided to or retrieved by the prover: Local File Context includes language syntax and semantic rules, while Repository Dependencies provides base types and generic lemmas. Ellipses (“…”) indicate that each context source contains many additional definitions. Color annotations trace dependencies from the theorem statement to its relevant context, highlighting the challenge: the prover must identify relevant definitions from a large local file and connect domain-specific rules with generic library lemmas.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Dataset statistics across repository categories. Category “Large” contains repositories with a context size exceeding 200k tokens. Values for Curated, Full Repo, and Trans. Deps represent the “average of averages”—the mean of individual repository averages for task token counts and transitive dependency counts, respectively. Repo Total represents the mean number of total transitive dependencies across all repositories within the category.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">System Specific Subset.</em>
Evaluation on Harmonic’s Aristotle system requires strict adherence to specific library versions, namely Mathlib v4.24.0. To ensure our benchmark is compatible with such systems, we filtered our full tasks set for version alignment and performed targeted manual refactoring to resolve versioning discrepancies. As the complexity of this engineering effort precluded scaling to the entire 500-task benchmark set, we collected a finalized subset of 100 fully-compatible tasks, enabling us to evaluate on the state-of-the-art specialized prover.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Task Composition.</em>
Each task consists of the target theorem, the local file context up to the theorem, all required local-repository definitions and helpful repository lemma declarations for stating and proving the target theorem, and the necessary library imports, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Dataset Construction ‣ 3 VeriSoftBench ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
Tasks are extracted without rewriting definitions or replacing local abstractions with equivalent standard-library formulations, preserving the original dependency structure of each proof.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Contextual Configurations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To study how provers use repository-local context under different levels of noise, we evaluate each task under two contextual configurations. Both configurations include the same <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">base context</em>, which includes: (i) the contents of the local file up to the target theorem (i.e., the definitions in scope) excluding the lemmas, and (ii) the external library (e.g., Mathlib, Std) imports and declarations required for the theorem statement to type-check.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Curated Context.</em>
The curated context mode provides the model with a focused set of dependencies designed to approximate the necessary background knowledge with minimal distraction for completing a proof.
In addition to the base context, it includes only the explicit repository dependencies: the specific definitions and lemmas from other files in the same repository that are directly invoked by the ground truth target theorem, and the transitively invoked definitions by any dependency in the context. To ensure the integrity of the evaluation and prevent models from mimicking domain-specific proof scripts, we elide the proof bodies of all provided lemmas and definitions. This configuration represents a best-case scenario where relevant premises have been pre-identified without leaking the actual proof, allowing us to isolate the model’s reasoning capabilities from its retrieval performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Full Context.</em> In this setting, the prover receives the entire repository library in addition to the base context. This includes all definitions and lemma/theorem statements across <em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">all files</em> in the repository. It is worth noting that the resulting context can be extremely long: among the 500 tasks, 119 come from repositories whose full-repository context exceeds hundreds of thousands of tokens, and one reaches hundreds of millions of tokens. Such instances are far beyond the effective context windows of current models, underscoring the need for reliable context-selection mechanisms. In our experiments, whenever the full context exceeds the model’s context window, we truncate it as needed. The detailed statistics in shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2.fig1" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Dataset Construction ‣ 3 VeriSoftBench ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph"><em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Preventing data leakage.</em></h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, both configurations are designed to avoid leaking the proof of the target theorem: we include only <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">preceding</em> context within the local file and never provide subsequent lemmas or proofs. Moreover, whenever we provide repository lemmas or definitions (either in the curated set or as part of the full repository), we include only their statements and elide proof bodies. Nevertheless, the Full Context configuration exposes the broader module ecosystem in which the theorem lives. As such, this ambient structural information can provide cues about recurring abstraction patterns or common proof structure that is largely absent in the curated configuration.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate performance on VeriSoftBench, we select a diverse set of models spanning frontier general-purpose LLMs and specialized formal reasoning systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate three primary baseline models that represent the current frontier of general-purpose reasoning and code generation: GPT-5.2, Claude-Opus-4.5, and Gemini-3-Pro. We also evaluate on Goedel-Prover-V2-32B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to include the perspective of specialized provers. We also evaluate Harmonic’s Aristotle Prover <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achim et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which is currently viewed as the state-of-the-art in formal mathematical verification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Evaluation pipeline</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate general-purpose LLMs using a generation-check-repair loop, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Evaluation pipeline ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. For each evaluation run, the model receives a task associated with the selected contextual configuration as input, and the evaluation proceeds in three stages: (1) we sample <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidate proof scripts from the model. Each candidate is generated as a tactical proof block intended to satisfy the target goal; (2) we wrap each generated script into its original file context and attempt verification using the Lean 4 compiler. To ensure a stable and efficient evaluation, the all task environments are pre-built prior to verification; we use the specific toolchain version associated with the source repository of each task and enforce a 300-second compilation timeout per candidate<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Large dependencies such as Mathlib are compiled once and cached per repository toolchain version.</span></span></span>; (3) for any failing script, we invoke the model for up to <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> repair rounds using the compiler error message, corresponding code lines from each error location, and the current proof state as feedback. A task is marked as “Solved” if any of the <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidates or their subsequent repairs pass verification. For specialized theorem-proving systems with an internal feedback loop (e.g., Goedel Prover v2 and Aristotle), we evaluate them as end-to-end systems rather than wrapping them in an external repair loop, as they already contain their own internal feedback loop.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18307v1/pipeline-flow.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/105;" width="286" height="105" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Evaluation Pipeline.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Data Configurations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider two variations of VeriSoftBench  that differ in scope and in the degree to which they accommodate prover-specific engineering constraints.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">VeriSoftBench-Full.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our primary evaluation setting is the full VeriSoftBench benchmark, consisting of 500 proof obligations. This setting is used for all models and provers that can consume our standard packaging of repository context.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">VeriSoftBench-Aristotle.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Aristotle imposes additional constraints on how repository context must be presented, e.g., requiring a pre-compiled environment rather than an in-prompt presentation of context. We use a restricted VeriSoftBench-Aristotle subset that includes 100 theorems curated to support their evaluation pipeline while preserving the repository-grounded nature of the tasks. When evaluating on VeriSoftBench-Aristotle, we employ a full-context variant that <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">additionally</em> includes local lemmas from the same file as the target theorem. We make this choice to avoid substantial project-specific engineering: removing same-file lemmas while retaining a pre-compiled environment typically requires repository restructuring and selective re-compilation. As a result, VeriSoftBench-Aristotle represents a simpler setting in which all lemma statements used by the ground-truth proof are available to the prover.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">

<tr id="S5.T3.fig1.3.7" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>VeriSoftBench evaluation results. Gödel-Prover-v2 was evaluated on <sup id="S5.T3.fig1.16" class="ltx_sup">†</sup> 496 tasks in the Curated Context configuration and <sup id="S5.T3.fig1.17" class="ltx_sup">‡</sup>44 tasks in the Full Context configuration to accommodate model-specific context window limitations; <sup id="S5.T3.fig1.18" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> for the VeriSoftBench<math id="S5.T3.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>Aristotle data setting, both models are evaluated on the <em id="S5.T3.fig1.19" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">variation</em> of the Full Context configuration as described in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Contextual Configurations ‣ 3 VeriSoftBench ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Model Performance.</em>
Table <a href="#S5.T3.fig1" title="Table 3 ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> summarizes the verification success rates across our two data settings (Full Set, Subset) and two contextual configurations (Curated Context, Full Context). Overall, performance is low, highlighting the inherent difficulty of the VeriSoftBench tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Under the Curated Context, the best-performing model, Gemini-3-Pro, achieves a success rate of <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="41.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>41.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">41.0\%</annotation></semantics></math>, followed by Claude Opus 4.5 at <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="31.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>31.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">31.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>. In the more challenging Full Repo Context, success rates decrease across all models; Gemini-3-Pro and Claude Opus 4.5 achieve <math id="S5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="34.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>34.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">34.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="23.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>23.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">23.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. GPT-5.2 reaches only <math id="S5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>. Notably, the specialized Gödel-Prover-v2 fails to solve any tasks (<math id="S5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math>) in the repository-scale setting. While such systems are highly optimized for solving standard mathematical problems, our results suggest they struggle with the tasks involving high density of domain specific local-repository abstractions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the VeriSoftBench-Partial split used to evaluate Aristotle, Aristotle attains a <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="69\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>69</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">69\%</annotation></semantics></math> success rate under the Full Context configuration. However, as noted in Section 4.4, this evaluation includes same-file helper lemmas that are used by the ground-truth proof. Since such local lemmas often encode key intermediate steps, their inclusion likely contributes substantially to Aristotle’s performance. We note that on this subset, Gemini-3-Pro achieves only slightly lower performance at 65%, indicating that this subset is substantially easier than the Full set. Quantifying how much of this performance persists when these proof-used local lemmas are withheld is an important direction for future evaluation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Comparison of Context Conditions.</em>
Table <a href="#S5.T3.fig1" title="Table 3 ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows a consistent performance drop when moving from Curated Context to Full Repo Context, although the gap is smaller than one might expect given the significant increase in contextual scope. In particular, the Curated Context is constructed to contain (approximately) the relevant repository dependencies with minimal distraction. As this Curated Context is synthesized using the ground truth proof (which would not be available to a prover at deployment time), the Full Repo Context may be viewed the more realistic setting: it requires the prover to identify relevant facts on its own without oracle guidance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The smaller-than-expected gap suggests that Full Context may provide compensating signals despite its much larger search space. Upon further analysis, we find that the full repository exposes additional hints that are absent in the curated setting: Even files that are not directly required for the target theorem often contain proofs with similar structure, lemmas, or recurring abstraction patterns. Seeing these nearby patterns may help a model anticipate useful intermediate lemmas or recognize common ways in which project-specific abstractions are typically applied, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18307v1/full-context.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/522;" width="476" height="522" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Although the target theorem is for 32-bit unsigned integers (U32), the context provides a structurally identical U64 soundness proof that factors bitwise equalities into a helper lemma and then applies it. Even though the actual soundness_to_u32 helper is not provided, this recurring abstraction pattern allows the model to anticipate its existence and shape and to replicate the same proof structure for the smaller word size.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Impact of High Contextual Dependency.</em> The difficulty of our benchmark is closely tied to its unusually high degree of contextual dependency. Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> quantifies the size of the dependency footprint. Theorems in VeriSoftBench directly reference only a modest number of items (2.3 library and 11.6 project dependencies on average), but their <em id="S5.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">transitive closure</em> expands to 11.2 library dependencies and 37.9 project dependencies <em id="S5.p6.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">per theorem</em>. In contrast, Verina tasks involve only shallow local dependencies (around 3 transitive dependencies on average), while PutnamBench theorems are entirely self-contained with zero project dependencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">However, dependency size alone does not fully capture structural difficulty. Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ VeriSoftBench: Repository-Scale Formal Verification Benchmarks for Lean" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows the dependency <em id="S5.p7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">nesting depth</em> — i.e., the length of the longest chain in the transitive dependency graph induced by referenced definitions and lemmas. The distribution reveals that many theorems require reasoning across long dependency chains: roughly half of the theorems have nesting depth <math id="S5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 5</annotation></semantics></math>, and around 10% exceed depth 12. This indicates that relevant information is often separated from the theorem statement by multiple layers of intermediate abstractions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p8.1" class="ltx_p">These two observations highlight an important distinction. A theorem may depend on dozens of definitions (large dependency size), but the key difficulty arises when those dependencies are arranged in long chains, where each step builds on the previous one. Our correlation analysis supports this interpretation: transitive dependency count is moderately negatively correlated with full-repository success (Spearman <math id="S5.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=-0.359,p&lt;0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.359</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=-0.359,p&lt;0.001</annotation></semantics></math>), while direct dependency count shows no significant correlation . This suggests that models struggle not with the presence of many nearby symbols, but with the need to follow multi-step derivation paths through layered abstractions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18307v1/figures/nesting_depth_log_scale.png" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/296;" width="476" height="296" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cumulative distribution of theorem dependency depth (log scale). Line shows mean across repositories; shading indicates ±1 std.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Comparison of dependency footprint across theorem proving benchmarks. Library dependencies count references to external libraries (e.g., Mathlib). Project dependencies count references to definitions and lemmas from the same repository (but excluding same-file helper lemmas). Direct refers to items explicitly referenced by the theorem statement or proof; transitive includes the recursive closure of all such dependencies.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.p9.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Comparison of Proof Patterns.</em> Beyond dependency structure, VeriSoftBench also differs from prior datasets in the proof patterns it induces. To compare proof styles across benchmarks in a controlled way, ground-truth proofs are not sufficient: many benchmarks do not provide them, and even when available, human-written proofs and prover-specific proof search can introduce stylistic confounders. We therefore perform a cross-dataset comparison (e.g., Verina vs. VeriSoftBench) using Gemini-3-Pro generated proofs that successfully verify in both datasets. This holds the prover constant and allows observed differences to be attributed primarily to the theorems themselves.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Under this controlled comparison, Verina and VeriSoftBench exhibit systematically different tactic profiles. In Verina, 43% of correct Gemini-generated proofs begin with <span id="S5.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">unfold</span>, and 81% close goals using <span id="S5.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">simp</span>, reflecting a pattern of definition unfolding followed by automation. Overall, automation tactics account for 51% of tactic usage in Verina proofs, and 21% of proofs are completed by essentially “one-shot” automation. In contrast, Gemini-generated proofs for VeriSoftBench rely far less on automation (21% of tactics). They also more often involve case analysis, with 67% exhibiting branching structure compared to 42% in Verina.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Automated Formal Verification.</em>
Formal verification provides strong assurance for software systems, but proof effort remains a significant bottleneck. Some tools, such as Dafny <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leino, 2010</a>)</cite> and Verus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lattuada et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, allow developers to write programs alongside their specifications, which are then discharged using automated SMT solvers. However, as full automation is not always possible, many high-assurance efforts rely on interactive theorem provers such as Lean, Rocq/Coq, and Isabelle, where developers manually construct machine-checked proofs in a tactic-guided workflow. This approach has enabled large-scale verified artifacts including CompCert <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leroy, 2009</a>)</cite>, seL4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klein et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, and CakeML <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2014</a>)</cite>. To reduce the engineering overhead of such efforts, prior work has proposed domain-specific verification frameworks, such as Iris <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jung et al., 2015</a>)</cite> for concurrent separation logic, Verdi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wilcox et al., 2015</a>)</cite> for distributed systems, and Loom <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gladshtein et al., 2026</a>)</cite> for constructing multi-modal verifiers. While these frameworks provide reusable abstractions and automation, they still require significant manual effort.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Benchmarks for correctness and verification.</em>
Early benchmarks such as HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and MBPP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite> validate LLM-generated code by unit tests on standalone, interview-style tasks but do not offer any formal correctness guarantee. More verification-oriented suites include DafnyBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loughridge et al., 2024</a>)</cite> which targets invariant and contract synthesis in Dafny and MiniCodeProps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lohn and Welleck, 2024</a>)</cite> which evaluates Lean proofs for small functional programs. A third line of work targets “veri-coding,” where models generate code together with machine-checked proofs. Examples include FVAPPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dougherty and Mehta, 2025</a>)</cite>, CLEVER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thakur et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and Verina <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Complementing these benchmarks, VeriSoftBench focuses on proof obligations embedded in repository-scale Lean developments with substantial project-specific context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">General ITP benchmarks.</em>
A large fraction of widely used benchmarks for Lean proof automation target formalized mathematics, spanning competition-level to textbook-style problems. MiniF2F <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>)</cite> focuses on Olympiad and contest problems, while ProofNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azerbayev et al., 2023</a>)</cite> pairs Lean 3 theorem statements with natural-language statements drawn from undergraduate mathematics texts. At larger scale, LeanDojo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> provides infrastructure and a benchmark extracted from Mathlib, and PutnamBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tsoukalas et al., 2024</a>)</cite> offers hand-written formalizations of Putnam Competition problems across multiple proof assistants. These suites are effective for measuring mathematical reasoning and library-based lemma selection, but they largely operate within a shared mathematical ecosystem such as MathLib where the core abstractions are globally available and recur across tasks. The miniCTX effort <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> moves toward more realistic, long-context theorem proving by supplying surrounding project context but it remains focused on mathematical theorems rather than repository-scale verification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">LLM-based prover systems.</em> Neural proof automation has progressed from early LLM-guided tactic prediction and search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lample et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polu and Sutskever, 2020</a>)</cite> to agentic systems that interact with a proof assistant and refine candidates using verifier feedback. For example, COPRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thakur et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and AxProver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> run an iterative generate-check-repair loop, using compiler feedback to correct failed steps. DSP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> complements this paradigm by constructing an intermediate sketch aligned with informal reasoning. A parallel line of work emphasizes premise selection and retrieval: LeanDojo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> provides a Lean environment and retrieval-based proving over large libraries and Rango <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thompson et al., 2025</a>)</cite> applies retrieval-augmented proving in Coq by retrieving both relevant premises and similar proofs. Alongside these agentic frameworks, specialized prover models combine large-scale pretraining on formal corpora with verifier-guided reinforcement learning. Examples in this category include Llemma <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azerbayev et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Kimina-Prover <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Gödel-Prover-V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and SeedProver <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Hilbert-Prover <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Varambally et al., 2025</a>)</cite> further integrates hierarchical decomposition with verifier feedback and informal reasoning. Despite significant advances, these systems are still predominantly evaluated on mathematics-centric benchmarks, motivating evaluation in repository-scale verification benchmarks like VeriSoftBench.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced VeriSoftBench, a benchmark suite of 500 Lean 4 proof obligations from open-source formal-methods developments, packaged to preserve project context and cross-file dependencies.
Our experiments show that current frontier LLMs and specialized provers achieve only modest success, with performance degrading as transitive dependency structure grows.
While curated context improves over full-repository context, the gains are limited and leave substantial headroom even under oracle-style context selection.
Overall, these results indicate that verification proofs pose challenges that are not well captured by Mathlib-centric mathematics benchmarks, and point to the need for methods that can navigate large repositories and reason effectively through layered, project-specific abstractions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine
Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none
which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>
